longForm.title: The Gulf of Tonkin Incident, 1964: What the NSA Knew and Didn't Say
longForm.excerpt: The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution of August 1964 authorized the escalation that turned an advisory mission into a war. It was based on two incidents. The first was real. The second almost certainly was not. Declassified NSA documents released in 2005 confirm that senior officials knew the difference.
paragraphs: The signals intelligence file for the night of 4 August 1964 runs to several hundred pages and was classified Top Secret Umbra for more than four decades. When the National Security Agency released a declassified history of its role in the Gulf of Tonkin incident in 2005 — produced internally by historian Robert Hanyok — the document confirmed what a number of researchers had long argued: the second attack on US naval vessels that night, the attack that President Lyndon Johnson used to obtain congressional authorization for the escalation of the Vietnam War, did not happen. What the file shows is not a conspiracy in the conventional sense. It shows something more instructive: a signals intelligence apparatus under pressure to confirm what its political superiors wanted to hear, and a systematic process of selecting the intercepts that supported the desired conclusion while setting aside those that did not.

The first incident, on 2 August 1964, was real. The USS Maddox (DD-731), conducting a signals intelligence collection mission in the Gulf of Tonkin under the cover of a routine patrol, was attacked by three North Vietnamese torpedo boats from the 135th Torpedo Squadron. The torpedo boats fired torpedoes and strafed the Maddox with 14.5mm guns. The Maddox returned fire, called in air support from USS Ticonderoga, and the attacking boats were driven off or damaged; one may have been sunk. No Americans were killed. The attack was a genuine North Vietnamese naval action, almost certainly triggered by South Vietnamese commando raids along the North Vietnamese coast — Operation 34A — that the North Vietnamese reasonably assumed the US was directing. The connection between 34A and the DESOTO patrols was a fact that the Johnson administration did not emphasize when it presented the incident to Congress.

The second incident, reported on the night of 4 August, was different in character from the beginning. The Maddox and the USS Turner Joy reported being under attack by torpedo boats in rough weather. The sonar operator on the Maddox, Petty Officer James Stockdale — not the aviator who would become a POW, a different man — reported multiple torpedo contacts. The Turner Joy reported firing on enemy vessels. Within hours, however, the commanding officer of the Maddox, Captain John Herrick, sent a message to the fleet that directly contradicted his earlier attack report: 'Review of action makes many reported contacts and torpedoes fired appear doubtful. Freak weather effects on radar and overeager sonarmen may have accounted for many reports. No actual visual sightings by Maddox. Suggest complete evaluation before any action taken.' Herrick's message was received. It was not the message that was forwarded to Washington.

Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara presented both incidents to President Johnson and subsequently to Congress as confirmed North Vietnamese attacks. The intercepted North Vietnamese communications that the NSA provided to support this presentation were, the Hanyok study later found, selectively edited. Signals that supported the conclusion that an attack had occurred were retained; signals that contradicted it, or suggested that the Vietnamese naval units were reporting on the earlier 2 August engagement rather than a new one, were excluded from the package sent to decision-makers. Whether this was deliberate deception or motivated selection of favorable evidence — which the documentary record does not fully resolve — the practical effect was the same: Congress and the President acted on an intelligence assessment that the NSA's own files contradicted.

The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution passed the Senate on 7 August 1964 by a vote of 88 to 2. The two dissenting votes were cast by Senators Wayne Morse of Oregon and Ernest Gruening of Alaska. Both had expressed doubts about the administration's account of the second incident. Morse went further, arguing on the floor that the Resolution was an unconstitutional delegation of war-making authority. The majority dismissed his objections. The Resolution authorized the President to take 'all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression,' language that the Johnson administration subsequently interpreted as authorization for the full-scale commitment of American ground forces, the sustained bombing of North Vietnam, and the expansion of the war that would eventually involve more than 500,000 American troops.

McNamara's own position on the second incident evolved over decades. In his 1995 memoir In Retrospect, he acknowledged that the second attack was 'doubtful' and that the decision to retaliate had been made on faulty intelligence. In Errol Morris's 2003 documentary The Fog of War, he went further, saying the attack 'didn't happen' and that he had been wrong to present it to Congress as established fact. These admissions, made decades after the Resolution had served its purpose, did not alter the legislative record or the casualties that followed from it. The question of whether McNamara and other senior officials knew at the time that the second attack was fabricated — or whether they genuinely believed the initial reports and suppressed Herrick's correction through bureaucratic inertia rather than deliberate deception — remains a matter of historical debate. The NSA's Hanyok study implies the former. McNamara's memoirs suggest the latter.

The Operation 34A context that the administration omitted from its congressional presentation has received significant scholarly attention. The covert raids on North Vietnamese coastal installations, conducted by South Vietnamese commandos with US logistics and direction, had been ongoing for months before August 1964. The raids were classified; the DESOTO patrols, which were collecting signals intelligence and were visible to North Vietnamese radar, were not classified. North Vietnamese commanders cannot have been unaware that the two programs overlapped. The attack on the Maddox on 2 August occurred two days after a particularly significant 34A raid. Whether the North Vietnamese naval attack was intended as a signal, a retaliation, or an opportunistic escalation is unclear from the available evidence. What is clear is that the United States was not conducting innocent freedom-of-navigation exercises in the Gulf of Tonkin during this period, and that the congressional resolution that authorized the war was obtained without that context being disclosed.

The archival record of the Gulf of Tonkin incident has been substantially clarified since 1995, and most serious historians now treat the second attack as fabricated or, at minimum, deeply uncertain. What the record cannot fully resolve is the chain of individual decisions — by radar operators, sonar operators, ship commanders, intelligence analysts, and cabinet officials — that converted Herrick's message of doubt into Johnson's message of certainty. The Hanyok study is the most complete documentary account, but it was itself classified until 2005, and the version released has redactions. The gap between what the NSA's files showed in August 1964 and what Johnson told Congress remains the most consequential intelligence failure in American political history, not because the intelligence community fabricated an incident, but because it provided policymakers with the analysis they wanted rather than the analysis the evidence supported.

shortForm.title: The USS Maddox and the Attack That Actually Happened
shortForm.excerpt: On 2 August 1964, the USS Maddox was genuinely attacked by North Vietnamese torpedo boats. The attack that followed two days later — the one that triggered the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution — almost certainly was not real. The distinction mattered enormously. It was not made.
paragraphs: The USS Maddox was a Gearing-class destroyer conducting a signals intelligence patrol in the Gulf of Tonkin on 2 August 1964. The patrol was officially a freedom-of-navigation exercise; the classified portion of its mission involved collecting North Vietnamese radar and communications signals — a DESOTO mission, in Navy parlance. Three North Vietnamese torpedo boats from the 135th Torpedo Squadron attacked the Maddox in international waters, firing two torpedoes that missed and strafing the ship. The Maddox returned fire, called in F-8 Crusaders from USS Ticonderoga, and the attacking boats were driven off. The engagement was brief and clearly documented. Nobody in the subsequent policy debate seriously disputed that the 2 August attack happened.

What the administration chose not to emphasize when presenting the 2 August attack to Congress was the context. South Vietnamese commandos, operating under the CIA- and MACV-directed Operation 34A, had raided North Vietnamese coastal installations on 30-31 July — two days before the Maddox attack. The raids were classified. The DESOTO patrols were not. The North Vietnamese had every reason to believe the two programs were connected, because they were. The torpedo boat attack on the Maddox was in all probability a calibrated North Vietnamese response to the 34A raids rather than an unprovoked act of aggression, but presenting it that way would have required disclosing a covert program that the administration was not prepared to acknowledge.

The operational log of the Maddox from 4 August — the night of the alleged second attack — was recovered and examined as part of the 2005 declassification review. Captain Herrick's message questioning the reality of the second attack, sent before Washington had publicly committed to a response, is in the log. The intercepts that the NSA provided to support the second attack are in the files, along with the intercepts that contradicted it. The 2 August attack, the one that was real, established the precedent that North Vietnamese naval forces were willing to engage US ships. The 4 August attack, the one that was almost certainly not real, established the legal basis for the war. The archival record makes clear which attack the administration found more useful.

onThisDay.headline: Union and Confederate Forces Fight at the Battle of Williamsburg During McClellan's Peninsula Campaign
onThisDay.summary: On 4 May 1862, Confederate forces under General James Longstreet and D.H. Hill fought a rearguard action against the pursuing Army of the Potomac at Williamsburg, Virginia, as General Joseph Johnston withdrew his army up the Peninsula toward Richmond. The battle cost the Union approximately 2,239 casualties and the Confederates approximately 1,560, delaying McClellan's advance by a day.
